teaser: Three meters of pure force: the painting where Futurism found its muscles.

lesson.text: Three meters. That is the width of this canvas, about 10 feet, and it stands 2 meters tall. Umberto Boccioni was 28 and had never painted anything close to that size. He spent the better part of a year on it, between 1910 and 1911, and called it his first truly Futurist picture.

Futurism was brand new. In 1909 the poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti had published a manifesto, a public declaration of aims, shouting that Italy must stop living off its museums and ruins. Speed, factories, crowds and electric light were the beauty of the new century. Boccioni signed up as the group's leading painter.

His subject was right outside his window. On the edge of Milan, whole districts were going up at once. He first titled the canvas Work. Only later did it become The City Rises, and that change tells you he wanted more than a picture of a building site.

lesson.title: Where is the city?
lesson.text: The title promises a city. It is there, pushed to the very top edge.

spots.title: Scaffolding
spots.text: A forest of poles and half-built brick walls runs along the upper edge. This is the rising city: new housing blocks going up on the outskirts of Milan.

spots.title: A chimney
spots.text: At far right a tall stack trails smoke across the pale sky. Industry is the reason all these buildings are needed.

spots.title: The tram
spots.text: At upper left, a tram glides past a line of poles. Electric streetcars were one of the modern wonders the Futurists loved.

lesson.text: So the modern city is a thin strip at the top. Everything below it, four fifths of the canvas, belongs to an animal as old as farming. A gigantic red draft horse surges across the middle, and men hang on to it as if they were caught in a flood.
For a movement that worshipped engines, this is an odd first triumph: there is no motor at the center of it. The power that raises Boccioni's modern city is horsepower in the literal sense.
Three movements collide in the center of the picture.

lines.label: The charge
lines.text: The red horse drives from right to left, head down. Your eye is dragged along its back against the usual left-to-right reading direction, so it feels like resistance.

lines.label: The blue wing
lines.text: The horse's collar, the padded yoke of a draft animal, flares up in blue like a wing or a blade. It is the darkest, coolest shape among all that red.

lines.label: The human diagonal
lines.text: The men lean at steep angles, arms flung out, feet braced. Their bodies form slanted bars pulling against the animals.

lesson.text: These workers have no faces to speak of. Boccioni is not painting portraits of laborers. He turns them into pure effort, each one a diagonal of strain, and lets their outlines melt into the horses and the air around them.
A second big horse comes in from the left, pale instead of red. Where is its head?

spots.title: The white horse
spots.text: It plunges in from the left edge with its neck arched, mane bristling in blue and white spikes. Its dark eye sits just below, near a worker's raised arm.

lesson.text: How do you paint force itself? Boccioni's answer was in the brushwork. He had learned Divisionism, a method of laying unmixed colors side by side in small strokes so that they blend in your eye instead of on the palette. Here he stretches those strokes into long threads that all flow one way, like iron filings near a magnet.

lesson.title: Threads of paint
lesson.text: Zoom into the surface. The energy is in the direction of the strokes.

spots.title: The red flank
spots.text: The horse's body is woven from strokes of red, orange and deep crimson, combed like fur in a wind. No outline holds it in.

spots.title: White heat
spots.text: In the lower right the ground dissolves into pale streaks of pink, yellow and blue. Dust and sunlight are painted with the same rushing threads as the muscles.

spots.title: A man in the current
spots.text: Find the round brown head and the bent back. The strokes run straight through him, so he seems carried by the same wave as the horse.

lesson.text: Boccioni did not paint things that move. He tried to paint the movement itself, by letting figures, animals and light dissolve into one direction of brushstrokes.
The first buyer was a musician. The pianist and composer Ferruccio Busoni saw the canvas when the Futurists exhibited in London in 1912 and paid 4,000 lire for it.

When it was first shown in Milan in 1911, the picture fit no familiar category. It was neither a realistic scene of labor nor a decorative allegory. Boccioni himself explained that he wanted a great synthesis of work, light and movement, a single image for the energy of a whole era.

Within a year he would visit Paris, discover Cubism and start breaking forms into sharp fragments. The soft, glowing threads of The City Rises never came back in his work. It stands at a hinge: the last picture of his youth and the first of the movement.
The canvas now hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York, which acquired it in 1951. It is one of the largest Futurist paintings anywhere.

One last detail belongs to life, not to the canvas. In 1916, serving in an Italian artillery regiment, Boccioni was thrown during a cavalry exercise and died the next day. He was 33. The painter of that unstoppable red horse was killed by a fall from one.

quiz.question: What was the painting first called?
quiz.explanation: Boccioni first exhibited it under the title Work.

quiz.question: Where is the actual city in the picture?
options: In a thin strip along the top edge
It is not shown at all
quiz.explanation: Scaffolding, a chimney and a tram are squeezed along the upper edge.

quiz.question: What is the blue shape rising from the red horse?
options: Its collar, flaring like a wing
quiz.explanation: The draft horse's padded collar becomes a blue wing or blade.

quiz.question: What is Divisionism?
options: Painting only in black and white
Placing unmixed colors side by side in small strokes
quiz.explanation: The colors blend in the viewer's eye instead of on the palette.

quiz.question: Who first bought The City Rises?
quiz.explanation: Busoni bought it in London in 1912.

quiz.question: How did Boccioni die?
options: After a fall from a horse
quiz.explanation: He was thrown during a cavalry exercise in 1916, at 33.

facts.text: The City Rises is about 3 meters wide.
facts.explanation: The canvas measures roughly 2 by 3 meters.

facts.text: The workers' faces are painted as detailed portraits.
facts.explanation: They are nearly faceless, reduced to diagonals of effort.

facts.text: An automobile engine drives the action at the center of the picture.
facts.explanation: The force at the center is a huge red draft horse.
